comparison: Perfect alignment on directional bias claims (C58-C60, C105-C108). Both evaluations support the findings on headwind preference during take-off. Peer reviewers acknowledged this as 'novel quantitative data' despite noting the interpretation relies on bird behavior without concurrent local wind measures. OpenEval similarly notes the inferential nature of C108 but finds the evidence compelling.

Perfect alignment on wave effects claims (C61-C70). Both evaluations strongly support these findings as novel insights. Peer reviewers emphasized that 'effects of wave height and interactions provide novel insight,' while OpenEval highlights the statistical rigor and large sample sizes. Both accept the acknowledged uncertainty about flapping frequency trends (C70).

Perfect alignment on wind effect mechanisms (C100-C104). Both evaluations support the aerodynamic explanations and contextualization with prior literature. Peer reviewers explicitly accepted the lift force mechanism as 'generally understood,' while OpenEval emphasizes appropriate citation support and acknowledgment of prior study limitations.

Strong alignment on wind condition data (C3-C4, C32-C37). OpenEval R5 focuses specifically on wind measurements, while peer R1 covers both wind and wave measurements (C38-C42). Both evaluations praise the high-quality dataset from animal-borne sensors. No concerns raised about environmental measurement validity.

Alignment on wave condition data (C4, C38-C42). OpenEval R6 addresses wave measurements specifically, while peer R1 encompasses both wind and wave data. Both support the quantitative measurements and methodology. OpenEval notes the inference about wave direction (C42) as reasonable; peer reviewers raised no concerns.

Strong alignment on running behavior data (C43-C49). Both evaluations support the quantitative findings. Peer reviewers noted lack of video validation for accelerometry interpretation as a weakness but still accepted the results. OpenEval emphasizes statistical rigor and internal consistency without noting this validation concern.

Strong alignment on flapping behavior data (C5, C50-C57). Both evaluations support the findings despite acknowledged detection limitations. Peer reviewers praised 'novel quantitative data' and noted the lack of video validation but accepted conclusions. OpenEval highlights methodological transparency in acknowledging limitations (C55-C56).

Strong alignment on statistical analysis of wind-wave interactions (C71-C81). Both evaluations support the sophisticated analytical approach addressing confounding. Peer reviewers emphasized these interaction effects as core novel findings that 'should revise understanding.' OpenEval details the statistical methods (VIF, AIC) and appropriately notes model uncertainty where AIC differences <2.

Alignment on model predictions and interaction effects (C82-C86). Both evaluations support these findings as part of the core contribution. Peer R5 emphasizes the novel insight into wave height effects. OpenEval appropriately notes these are model predictions with substantial uncertainty in confidence intervals, particularly for extreme conditions.

Strong alignment on primary conclusions about wave facilitation (C6-C8). Both evaluations strongly support these as the main contribution. Peer reviewers stated findings 'should revise understanding' and authors 'achieved their objectives.' OpenEval emphasizes these claims are well-supported by multiple lines of evidence from the comprehensive analysis.

Alignment on overall study conclusions (C8). Both evaluations support the synthesis of findings. Peer R6 emphasizes broader implications for understanding climate change effects and setting 'new standards' in integrating movement and environmental data. OpenEval focuses on how C8 appropriately synthesizes the specific findings.

Alignment on methodological and scientific contributions (C87, C122). Both evaluations support these conclusions about the study's novelty and approach. Peer reviewers praised the work as setting 'new standards' with 'heuristic insights.' OpenEval notes 'experimentally demonstrated' (C122) might overstate the observational nature, but peer reviewers did not raise this concern.

Alignment on synthesis of wind effects and future research directions (C96-C99). Both evaluations support these conclusions. Peer R6 emphasizes implications for climate change understanding. OpenEval highlights the logical inference that wind is not the only factor (C98) based on observations of take-offs in weak winds combined with demonstrated wave effects.

Strong alignment on research context and motivation (C1-C2, C9-C16). Both evaluations support the framing of the research gap. Peer reviewers endorsed the motivation for using animal-borne sensors to study 'small-scale environmental conditions.' OpenEval emphasizes the claims are well-supported by citations and accurately characterize limitations in current methods.

Strong alignment on methodological details and data collection (C130-C136). Both evaluations praise the dataset quality and methodology. Peer reviewers noted the large birds can carry substantial equipment 'without creating significant impact.' OpenEval highlights specific quantitative details and appropriate citation support for lack of negative impacts (C136).

Alignment on sample sizes and data filtering (C27-C31). Both evaluations support the methodological rigor. Peer R11 praises the 'compelling high quality dataset.' OpenEval emphasizes the logical progressive filtering and appropriate statistical quality control, finding the criteria for inclusion/exclusion well-justified.

Alignment on temporal dynamics and flapping patterns (C88-C92). Both evaluations support these inferences about energetic costs and timing. Peer reviewers accepted the interpretations without challenge, noting the paper addresses 'bio-energetics.' OpenEval notes these are reasonable inferences reconciling current data with prior literature, though not directly verifiable.

Alignment on flapping compensation mechanisms (C113-C114). Both evaluations support these inferences about energetic implications. Peer R7 groups these with other energetic interpretations and finds them convincing. OpenEval emphasizes consistency with aerodynamic principles and the observed inverse relationship between wind speed and flapping.

Divergence on wave-slope soaring mechanisms (C115-C121). OpenEval supports these claims as appropriately reviewing literature and providing plausible mechanistic explanations. Peer R9 rates these as UNCERTAIN, noting reviewers did not explicitly evaluate the speculative mechanisms despite praising the demonstration that waves aid take-off.

Divergence on mechanistic uncertainty (C123-C126). OpenEval supports the acknowledgment of uncertainty as demonstrating scientific honesty and appropriately identifying future research questions. Peer R9 rates as UNCERTAIN because reviewers neither affirmed nor challenged these speculations about mechanisms, despite the authors' own caution.

OpenEval R2 addresses background literature on energetic costs and dynamic soaring (C17-C26). No corresponding peer review evaluation found. These claims provide context cited from previous research rather than novel findings from the current study.

OpenEval R16 addresses inferences about land bird comparisons (C93-C95). No corresponding peer review evaluation found. These claims cite previous research on land birds and make speculative inferences about seabirds, with appropriate calls for further research.

OpenEval R19 addresses caveats about wind speed estimates and atmospheric boundary layers (C109-C112). No corresponding peer review evaluation found. These claims acknowledge methodological limitations regarding surface wind estimates, demonstrating scientific caution.

OpenEval R23 addresses climate change implications (C129). No corresponding peer review evaluation found. This claim synthesizes energetic costs with current findings to highlight broader significance, though peer reviewers did mention climate change implications in their general comments (R6).
